players.product: leading-edge wafer fab (N3/N2 GAA logic dies)

quarterly_data.signal: Q4 2025 results (CFO): revenue increased 5.7% sequentially in NT and, in U.S. dollar terms, 1.9% sequentially to 33.7 billion (the transcript prints the unit as TWD inside an 'In U.S. dollar terms' sentence), slightly ahead of guidance. Gross margin rose 2.8 percentage points sequentially to 62.3%, beating the high end of guidance by 130 basis points on better-than-expected cost improvement; operating margin 54%; EPS TWD 19.5; ROE 38.8%. Node mix: 3-nanometer 28% of wafer revenue, 5-nanometer 35%, 7-nanometer 14%; advanced technologies (7-nanometer and below) 77%. Platforms: HPC increased 4% quarter-over-quarter to 55% of revenue; smartphone increased 11% to 32%.
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 revenue 33.7 billion in U.S. dollar terms (+1.9% sequentially); gross margin 62.3%; operating margin 54%; 3-nanometer 28% / 5-nanometer 35% / 7-nanometer 14% of wafer revenue; HPC 55% of revenue

quarterly_data.signal: Full year 2025: revenue increased 35.9% in U.S. dollar terms to 122 billion (31.6% in NT dollar terms to TWD 3.8 trillion), outperforming the Foundry 2.0 industry (all logic wafer manufacturing, packaging, testing, mask making and others), which grew 16%. Gross margin rose 3.8 percentage points to 59.9%, operating margin 50.8%, EPS TWD 66.25 (+46.4%), ROE 35.4%. Advanced technologies were 74% of wafer revenue, up from 69% in 2024 (3-nanometer 24%, 5-nanometer 36%, 7-nanometer 14%). HPC revenue increased 48% year-over-year to 58% of 2025 revenue. Capital expenditures were USD 40.9 billion (USD 29.8 billion in 2024); free cash flow TWD 1 trillion.
quarterly_data.figure: FY2025 revenue +35.9% in U.S. dollar terms to 122 billion; gross margin 59.9%; operating margin 50.8%; HPC +48% to 58% of revenue; advanced technologies 74% of wafer revenue (69% in 2024)

quarterly_data.signal: Guidance given on this call: Q1 2026 revenue between USD 34.6 billion and USD 35.8 billion (a 4% sequential / 38% year-over-year increase at the midpoint), gross margin between 63% and 65% (up 170 basis points to 64% at the midpoint on cost improvement and higher utilization, partly offset by overseas-fab dilution) and operating margin between 54% and 56%, at USD 1 to TWD 31.6. Full year 2026: C.C. Wei forecast revenue to increase by close to 30% in U.S. dollar terms, versus 14% growth forecast for the Foundry 2.0 industry, while flagging uncertainty from tariff policies and rising component prices; overall utilization to moderately increase; depreciation up by high teens percentage, mainly from the 2-nanometer ramp; effective tax rate 17% to 18%. Pricing 'will remain strategic, not opportunistic'; the CFO said pricing benefits in recent years were 'just enough to cover the inflation cost from tools, equipment, materials, labor'. Non-AI: with higher memory prices C.C. Wei expects PC and smartphone 'unit growth will be very minimal', but TSMC supplies most high-end smartphones, which are less sensitive, networking processors and switches 'still grow very strong', and customers 'continue to give us a very healthy forecast this year and next year'.
quarterly_data.figure: Q1 2026 revenue between USD 34.6 billion and USD 35.8 billion; gross margin between 63% and 65%; operating margin between 54% and 56%; FY2026 revenue growth close to 30% in U.S. dollar terms

quarterly_data.signal: 2026 capital budget set between USD 52 billion and USD 56 billion (USD 40.9 billion in 2025, USD 29.8 billion in 2024): about 70% to 80% to advanced process technologies, about 10% to specialty technologies and about 10% to 20% to advanced packaging, testing, mask making and others. The CFO said capex totaled USD 167 billion over the last 5 years and that leading-node capacity is getting costlier: the capex to build 1,000 wafer per month capacity of N2 is 'substantially higher' than for N3, and the capex per k for A14 will be even higher. C.C. Wei: 'we have to invest about USD 52 billion to USD 56 billion for the CapEx... If we didn't do it carefully, and that would be big disaster to TSMC for sure', which is why he checked demand directly with the cloud service providers.
quarterly_data.figure: 2026 capital budget between USD 52 billion and USD 56 billion (2025: USD 40.9 billion); 70% to 80% advanced process; 10% to 20% advanced packaging, testing, mask making and others

quarterly_data.signal: Leading-edge supply stays tight. C.C. Wei: 'The capacity is very tight. We work very hard to narrow the gap so far. Probably this year, next year, we have to work extremely hard to narrow the gap' and 'Our headache right now, if I can call it a headache, is a demand and supply gap.' Because a new fab takes 2 to 3 years to build, the 2026 capex contributes 'almost none' this year and 'a little bit' to 2027: 'we actually are looking for 2028, 2029 supply. And we hope at that time that the gap will be narrow.' For 2026 and 2027 the focus is short-term output through productivity improvement; TSMC is also converting N5 capacity to support N3 wherever necessary, optimizing capacity across nodes (flexible support among N7, N5 and N3) and putting forward existing fab schedules in Taiwan and Arizona.
quarterly_data.figure: Capacity 'very tight'; 'this year, next year' spent narrowing the gap; new-fab supply aimed at 2028, 2029

quarterly_data.signal: Global footprint update. Arizona: the first fab entered high-volume production in 4Q '24 and yield and defect density are 'almost equal to Taiwan'; construction of the third fab has started; TSMC is applying for permits to begin construction of the fourth fab (and the first advanced packaging fab), building toward an independent giga-fab cluster for leading-edge smartphone, AI and HPC customers ('We are going to expand many fabs over there'). Japan: the first Kumamoto specialty fab started volume production in late 2024 with very good yield, and construction of the second fab has started. Germany: construction of the Dresden specialty fab is progressing. Taiwan: preparing multiple 2-nanometer fabs in both Hsinchu and Kaohsiung Science Park, with continued investment in leading edge and advanced packaging facilities. Mature nodes: 'we reduced our 8-inch wafers capacity and 6-inch', while continuing to support those customers.
quarterly_data.figure: Arizona third fab under construction; permits in process for fourth fab; Arizona yield and defect density 'almost equal to Taiwan'

quarterly_data.signal: N2 family roadmap: N2P, an extension of N2 with further performance and power benefits, is scheduled for volume production in the second half of this year (2026); A16, featuring superpower rail (SPR) and 'best suitable for specific HPC products with complex signal route and dense power delivery network', is on track for volume production in the second half 2026. C.C. Wei said 'almost all the innovators are working with TSMC' on N2 and A16, demand from smartphone and HPC AI is strong with a fast ramp expected in 2026, and N2, N2P, A16 and derivatives will make N2 'another large and long-lasting node' ('the third one will be N2 something'). The CFO said 2-nanometer 'will be a bigger node than 3-nanometer from the start' in revenue dollars. C.C. Wei on node longevity: leading-edge customers arrive in 'the first wave, the second wave, the third wave', so node revenue does not decrease after reaching its peak.
quarterly_data.figure: N2P and A16 volume production in second half 2026; 2-nanometer 'a bigger node than 3-nanometer from the start'

players.product: N3/N2-class processed logic wafers (Rubin GPU + Vera CPU dies)

quarterly_data.signal: AI demand backdrop: revenue from AI accelerators was high teens percent of TSMC's total revenue in 2025. TSMC raised its forecast for AI accelerator revenue growth to approach a mid- to high 50s percent CAGR for 2024 to 2029, and now expects overall long-term revenue growth to approach 25% CAGR in U.S. dollar terms over the same period, with AI accelerators the largest contributor to incremental growth. C.C. Wei said he spent the last 3, 4 months talking to all the cloud service providers, who 'show me the evidence that the AI really help their business'; the customers' customers are 'reaching out directly to request the capacity', and engagement lead time is now at least 2 to 3 years in advance. On data-center power, CSPs told him they planned power supply 5, 6 years ago and that 'silicon from TSMC is a bottleneck'; in his words, 'still the bottleneck is TSMC's wafer supply. Not the power consumption, not yet.' He pointed to his customers' cadence 'from Hopper to Blackwell to Rubin, that almost double, triple their performance'.
quarterly_data.figure: AI accelerators high teens percent of 2025 revenue; AI accelerator revenue CAGR to approach mid- to high 50s percent (2024 to 2029); overall revenue CAGR to approach 25% in U.S. dollar terms

quarterly_data.signal: Advanced packaging sizing (CFO): revenue contribution from advanced packaging in 2025 was 'close to 10%. It's about 8%', expected to be 'slightly over 10%' in 2026 and to grow faster than the corporate average over the next 5 years. In the past advanced packaging capex was lower than 10% of the total; now advanced packaging together with mask making and others takes between 10% to 20% of the 2026 budget, so 'the investment amount is higher', invested in 'areas in advanced packaging where our customers need' (asked about 3DIC, SoIC and panel-level, the CFO said 'basically, we continue to invest'). Capacity: TSMC is applying for permits to build its first advanced packaging fab in Arizona and will keep investing in advanced packaging facilities in Taiwan over the next few years.
quarterly_data.figure: Advanced packaging about 8% of 2025 revenue; slightly over 10% expected in 2026; 10% to 20% of 2026 capex (with mask making and others)
